questions.q: Explain the modern theory of the origin of the universe and the solar system.

answer.text: The most widely accepted explanation for the origin of the universe is the Big Bang theory, also called the expanding universe hypothesis. It holds that about 13.7 billion years ago all matter was concentrated in an extremely small and dense point, which exploded and began to expand. As it expanded and cooled, matter formed into galaxies and stars. Observations show that galaxies are still moving apart, so the universe continues to expand.

The solar system is explained by the nebular hypothesis, first proposed by Laplace and Kant and later revised. It suggests that the Sun and planets formed about five billion years ago from a rotating cloud of gas and dust called a nebula. Material gathered at the centre to form the Sun, while the rest condensed into planets through the accretion of small bodies.

answer: These theories together account for the birth of the universe and our solar system.

questions.q: How did the planets of the solar system form according to modern understanding?

answer.text: are thought to have formed from the same cloud of gas and dust that gave birth to the Sun, in a process linked to the nebular idea.

list: A rotating cloud (nebula) contracted, and its centre became the Sun while the rest formed a disc around it
Within this disc, tiny particles collided and stuck together to form small bodies (planetesimals)
The planetesimals collided and combined to build up the planets over time
The inner planets became small and rocky, and the outer ones large and gaseous, giving the solar system its present form

questions.q: How was the Moon formed, and how is the Earth's early evolution understood?

answer.text: is believed to have formed from a giant collision, not to have been captured or born with the Earth.

list: A Mars-sized body is thought to have struck the young Earth
The debris thrown out went into orbit and gathered together to form the Moon
It was initially very hot and largely molten, and the heavier material sank to form the core while lighter material rose
This 'differentiation' gave the Earth its layered structure; gases released from the interior formed the early atmosphere and, later, water
